title: The Toucan and the cluster
caption: The open star cluster NGC 299, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 299 · constellation Tucana · about 200000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Hubble captures NGC 299, an open star cluster sitting in the Small Magellanic Cloud a little less than 200,000 light-years from us. It lies in the southern constellation of Tucana, the Toucan, famous for the Tucana Dwarf Galaxy and the cluster 47 Tucanae, but home to many quieter beauties too.

Open clusters are collections of stars weakly held together by gravity, all born from a single large cloud of molecular gas and dust. As a result, the stars share the same age and composition. They differ in mass, though, because they formed in different parts of the cloud.

That combination is what makes such a cluster valuable. With age and composition fixed, astronomers can see how mass alone shapes a star's life, since the way stars form and evolve is thought to depend strongly on their mass. The cluster becomes a natural laboratory, and seen through an instrument like Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, a striking one.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.04 x 1.51 arcminutes) and distance (200000 light years), the frame spans roughly 119 × 88 light-years. Its light set out about 200,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the cluster through visible and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble resolves individual stars in a cluster in another galaxy.

explore: 47 Tucanae, also in Tucana, is the second-brightest globular cluster in the night sky.
